hardinessNote: Hardy in most places throughout the UK, approximately -15 to -10°C.
visual: Upright sprays of scented bright yellow flowers over spiny pinnate leaves · winter bee food
water: Water regularly while establishing; copes with dry shade once settled.
prune: Little needed; cut leggy stems back hard after flowering to thicken it.
toxicity: Leaflets carry sharp spines, so wear gloves when handling. Berries and roots contain berberine and may cause a mild stomach upset if a child eats many; the ASPCA lists common Mahonia as safe for dogs and cats.
cvs: 'Charity' – spreading sprays, the classic · 'Winter Sun' – denser, more compact upright sprays · 'Buckland' – longer, arching sprays
resilience: Tough and very shade tolerant; trouble-free apart from occasional leaf spot, rust or mildew.
uses: Shady borders · woodland planting · winter interest · security planting
foliage: evergreen; long pinnate leaves of 17–21 spiny dark green leaflets
uncertain: peak: sources disagree — RHS 'autumn and winter', a blog November, a nursery Oct–Dec, Gardeners' World Jan–Feb; Nov-Feb matches the deck's 'Charity' card
height/spread: RHS gives 2.5–4 m in 10–20 years; Burncoose 5 × 4 m and Gardens Illustrated 4 × 4 m, so the RHS figure is used
toxicity: no RHS statement found; berberine content is general to Mahonia; ASPCA non-toxic listing is for M. aquifolium, not this hybrid
aspect, soil, thirst, ratings: carried from the RHS profile and the genus siblings in the deck, not a cultivar-specific source
clay: inferred from genus tolerance of moist loam/clay, not stated for this cultivar
container: only while young; it outgrows a pot within a few years
